The applications were adjourned pending the outcome of a reference to the European Court of Justice (“ECJ”) pursuant to Article 177 of the Treaty of Rome by the English High Court on the question of the applicability of the Council Directive on the Implementation of the Principle of Equal Treatment for Men and Women.

The applicant had been involved in a steady relationship with a civilian partner for about 30 months prior to June 1994. In early June 1994 the applicant was informed that the Royal Navy Special Investigations Branch (‘the service police’) had been given his name anonymously in connection with an allegation of homosexuality. The applicant was interviewed on 13 June 1994 by personnel from the service police about his sexual orientation for approximately twenty minutes. He was asked, inter alia, whether he had had homosexual contact with service personnel (at least four questions on this subject), what type of sexual relations he had. had with a particular person, when and where this had occurred, about his current relationship and whether his parents knew of his homosexuality.

In early June 1994 the applicant was informed that the Royal Navy Special Investigations Branch (“the service police”) had been given his name anonymously in connection with an allegation of homosexuality. The applicant admitted to his commanding officer that he was homosexual. He was then asked, inter alia, whether he had had homosexual contact with service personnel (at least four questions on this subject) He was also asked about his current relationship and whether his parents knew of his homosexuality. A search was normally completed but the search did not occur. The case was heard by the Crown Prosecution Service and the jury returned a verdict of not guilty.

The first applicant joined the Royal Navy Reserve as a radio operator in 1982. He became a midshipman in the executive branch of the navy in 1983. In 1994 the applicant attained the rank of lieutenant-commander. He was interviewed by the service police about his sexual orientation on 13 June 1994. The applicant was asked, inter alia, whether he had had homosexual contact with service personnel (at least four questions on this subject) He was also asked about his current relationship and whether his parents knew of his homosexuality. He then confirmed that he was homosexual, acknowledging that he had been a practising homosexual since his teenage years.

The second applicant joined the Royal Navy, enlisting for twenty-two years in 1989. He was discharged in 1995 for his sexual orientation. His commission was removed and most of the bonus which he had received with that promotion was recouped by the naval authorities (£4,875 out of £6,000) His term of service would otherwise have terminated in 2009, with the possibility of renewal. The applicant was also asked of the applicant “purely as a matter of interest, although it’s a personal thing’ whether the applicant was HIV-positive. The Admiralty Board informed him that it had decided to terminate his commission and to discharge him, administratively, from the navy with effect from 17 January 1995.

The ground for his discharge was his sexual orientation. On 20 February 1989 Mr Beckett (the second applicant) joined the Royal Navy, enlisting for twenty-two years.

The applicant had been refused time off to deal with a personal matter. He spoke with the chaplain, to whom he admitted his sexual orientation. He was then called for interview by the service police. The interview was suspended pending the search of his locker. During the search, slides (of himself, his partner and some of his service friends) and personal postcards were seized. The applicant was then questioned about his first and current homosexual relationship which began in December 1992. Details were sought as to how and what he did when he realised he was homosexual. He also was asked what sort of feelings he had for a man, whether he had been “touched up” or “abused” as a child.

The applicant’s administrative discharge was approved on the basis of his homosexuality. Ministry of defence, ex parte Smith and Others 2 Weeky Law Reports 305) and granted leave to apply for judicial review of the decisions to discharge them from the armed Forces. The application was dismissed on 6 December 1994 and the applicants were discharged.

High Court dismissed the application for judicial review, Lord Justice Simon Brown giving the main judgment of the court. All four of the applicants had exemplary service records, some with reports written in glowing terms. There was no reason to doubt that, but for their discharge, they would have continued to perform their service duties entirely efficiently and with the continued support of their colleagues. In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer and added, “I doubt whether most of those present in court throughout the proceedings now believe otherwise”

The High Court dismissed the application for judicial review, Lord Justice Simon Brown giving the main judgment of the court. He noted that the cases illustrated the hardships resulting from the absolute policy against homosexuals in the armed forces. In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer and added, “I doubt whether most of those present in court throughout the proceedings now believe otherwise.” But he concluded that the conventional Wednesbury principles, adapted to a human rights context, should be applied. Accordingly, where fundamental human rights were being restricted, the Minister of Defence needed to show there was an important competing interest to justify the restriction.

He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer and added, “I doubt whether most of those present in court throughout the proceedings now believe otherwise” However, having considered arguments as to the test to be applied in the context of these judicial review proceedings, Simon Brown LJ concluded that the conventional Wednesbury principles, adapted to a human rights context, should be applied.

The Master of the Rolls noted that the case concerned innate qualities of a very personal kind. He considered that the greater the policy content of the decision and the more remote the subject matter of a decision from ordinary judicial experience, the more hesitant the court had to be in holding a decision to be irrational. While the court must properly defer to the expertise of responsible decision-makers, it must not shrink from its fundamental duty to ‘do right to all manner of people’ He concluded that the policy could not be considered “irrational” at the time the applicants were discharged from the armed forces, finding that the threshold of irrationality was “a high one” and that it had not been crossed in this case.

He also accepted that the Equal Treatment Directive did not apply to complaints in relation to sexual orientation.

The court found that Mr Lustig-Prean and Mr Beckett had been unfairly dismissed from their jobs.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 25379/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a British national, Mr Geoffrey Twizell (‘the applicant’), on 7 June 2002. The President of the Chamber to which the case had been allocated, decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The United Kingdom Government were represented by their Agent, Mr C. Whomersley of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London. By a decision of 12 November 2002 the Court decided to communicate the application.

Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. U.K. Government represented by their Agent, Mr C. Whomersley of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London. By a decision of 12 November 2002 the Court decided to communicate the application. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the convention, the President of the Chamber to which the case had been allocated, decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Court ruled that the application should be allowed to go ahead and that the case should be heard by the Court of Appeal.

The applicant was born in 1941 and lives in France. His wife died on 26 March 2001. They had no children from the marriage. His claim for widows’ benefits under the new system in place as from 9 April 2001 was made on 4 May 2001. On 10 July 2001 the applicant appealed. Reconsideration took place on 23 July 2001 and the decision remained unchanged. On 15 November 2001 his appeal was heard and dismissed by an Appeal Tribunal. On 20 February 2002 the applicant was informed that his request had been disallowed. He did not appeal further as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail. No such social security or tax benefits were payable to widowers under United Kingdom law.

The applicant appealed to the Vorarlberg Independent Administrative Panel (Unabhängiger Verwaltungssenat) The panel dismissed the applicant's appeal and ordered him to pay ATS 90 by way of contribution to the costs of the proceedings. The District Authority found that the information supplied by the applicant had been inaccurate.

Their purpose is to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 para. 3 (e) and 14 (art. 6-3-e, art. 14) of the Convention. The President of the Court drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of five of the seven judges called upon to sit as members of the Chamber. On 21 November, Mr. Balladore Pallieri, acting in pursuance of Rule 24 para. 4, granted himself exemption from sitting on the case. Mr. Wiarda, the Vice-President of the Court, became a full member of the Chamber. The Government filed their memorial on 30 January 1978. The Secretary to the Commission advised the Deputy Registrar on 17 April that the Delegates had decided not to file a memorial in reply. On 8 May, he communicated to the Registrar a note containing ‘the applicants’ observations on the question of the application of Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention’ and Mr. Koç’s observations that his case be severed from the other two. Three applicants were charged before the German courts with the commission of various criminal offences. Since they were not sufficiently familiar with the language of the country, they were assisted by an interpreter in accordance with German law. After conviction they were ordered, amongst other things, to pay the costs of the proceedings, including the interpretation costs. They consider that the inclusion of this latter item is contrary to, inter alia, Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention. The Commission produces to the Court certain documents referred to by the Principal Delegate at the hearings. These documents were the subject of a letter, received on 16 August, from the Agent of the Government. Interpretation costs are part of the costs of the proceedings. They are made up of “the fees (Gebühren) and expenses of the Treasury’. In the event of acquittal or of proceedings being discontinued, the Treasury in principle bears the costs. If an individual concerned is convicted, he has to pay the costs, but only such proportion thereof as relates to the criminal charges upheld by the court. The text has not been interpreted and applied by the German courts in a uniform way. Certain courts read it as embodying an obligation for the Treasury to pay costs. For the purposes of compensation, interpreters shall be treated as experts’ Gerhard W. Luedicke was convicted of a road traffic offence. He was fined DM 900 and ordered to pay the costs of the proceedings. He appealed against this assessment of costs, which he argued was contrary to Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention in so far as it concerned payment of the interpretation costs. The appeal was rejected and the matter was referred to the Bielefeld Regional Court. Mr. Luingicke then applied to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) to have the costs in question for all time and in all cases. The ECHR ruled in his favour and ordered the costs to be paid. Mohammed Belkacem is an Algerian citizen, born in 1954. After completing his apprenticeship as a locksmith in Algeria, he rejoined his father in the Federal Republic of Germany where he followed various occupations. In December 1973, he was involved in a dispute in a Berlin night-club during which another client lost his coat. He paid the costs of the proceedings, including the interpretation costs. In Germany, Article 6 (art. 6) of the Convention ... is to guarantee certain fundamental rights to everyone faced with criminal proceedings. Under German procedural law, however, no accused person need make advance payment for the cost of interpreters. Berlin-Tiergarten Juvenile Court convicted him of assault occasioning bodily harm. He was sentenced to four weeks’ imprisonment (Dauerarrest) and a fine of DM 500. Mr. Belkacem filed an “immediate appeal’ against the order as to costs insofar as the interpretation costs had been included in the award. He submitted that Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention granted him exemption from payment of the costs in question. On 13 June 1974, the Berlin Regional Court dismissed the appeal. The Regional Court reasoned that, since no assessment of costs had yet been made, there had been no decision capable of being challenged. Arif Koç, a Turkish citizen born in 1940, has been employed in the Federal Republic of Germany in various trades, including mining and the construction industry. On 6 December 1973, the Assize Court attached to the Regional Court (Schwurgericht beim Landgericht) at Aachen convicted Mr. Koç of causing grievous bodily harm. He was sentenced to a year’s imprisonment, but the balance of his sentence remaining after allowance had been made for his detention on remand was commended. He has not been required to pay the costs in question since, at the request of the Government, the relevant Berlin authorities (Landesjustizverwaltung) have suspended recovery. Assize Court held that the “free’ assistance of an interpreter is to be understood as being free once and for all time. Cologne Court of Appeal set aside the Assize Court’s judgment insofar as it related to the interpretation costs. A fair trial is guaranteed in this respect insofar as the accused must be assisted by the interpreter he needs, the Court of appeal said. The object of the Convention is to secure human rights and fundamental freedoms against arbitrary State action and to place them under the protection of supranational law, the court said in its ruling. It is not its purpose to go further and alter the national legal systems, it added. According to the payment vouchers (Kassenanweisungen), the fees paid to the interpreter amounted to DM 311.50 for the hearing on 4 December 1973. The applicant was not served with a notice to pay the costs for which he was liable, including the interpretation costs, since it was noted that he had a wife and four children to support, that his income was modest and that there was thus no prospect of recovering the costs. A second decision to this effect was taken by the same official on 20 December 1977. This decision recorded that the applicant was living in Turkey that his address was unknown and that recovery of the costs, being doomed to failure, should be waived. The Commission declared Mr. Luedicke’s application admissible on 11 March 1976. The applications of Mr. Belkacem and Mr. Koç were also declared admissible. In its report of 18 May 1977, the Commission expressed the opinion that the decisions concerning the interpreter's costs in the applicants’ cases were in breach of Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention. The Government of Germany requested that the Court strike the case out of its list insofar as the applicant Koç was concerned. The Commission declared by twelve votes to one, that it was not necessary to pursue its examination of the case under Article 14.

James Malone was charged with a number of offences relating to dishonest handling of stolen goods. His trial, which took place in June and August 1978, resulted in his being acquitted on certain counts and the jury disagreeing on the rest. He was retried on the remaining charges between April and May 1979. Following a further failure by the jury to agree, he was once more formally arraigned; the prosecution offered no evidence and he was acquitted. On 28 February 1979, the Vice-Chancellor, Sir Robert Megarry, dismissed the applicant’s claim (Malone v. Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis (No. 2), [1979] 2 All England Law Reports 620; also reported at [ 1979] 2 Weekly Law Reports 700).

The applicant was born in 1953 and lives in Trabzon. He signed a contract with POAŞ (Petrol Ofisi A.Ş.), formerly a State-owned enterprise, for the operation of a petrol station. Having obtained a construction permit and carried out certain building work at the site, the applicant applied for an operations licence but was refused on grounds of safety, due to the proximity of the petrol station to a railway. The applicant lodged an action with the Ankara Commercial Court for the termination of the contract, which he claimed was null and void. He also requested the reimbursement of his expenditure, together with interest (case no. 1997/305).

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42317/98) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that neither he nor his legal representative were given the opportunity to address the magistrates' court prior to the imposition of a binding over order in respect of which he was later committed to prison. By a decision of 21 October 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court)

Divisional Court (Lord Justice Simon Brown and Mr Justice Mance) agreed that the binding over order had been procedurally irregular. A surety required the separate approval of the court as to his suitability. This was outside the control of the person to be bound over. This could have drastic consequences for him where, as in the present case, it resulted in his serving a period of imprisonment imposed as an alternative. The Magistrates needed to take particular care lest, in effect, they imposed a binding order which amounted to an automatic sentence of imprisonment without appreciating what they were doing. A defendant ought not to be put at peril of a prison sentence in default of finding a surety unless he had first been specifically invited to address the magistrates' court upon that point.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42317/98) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that neither he nor his legal representative were given the opportunity to address the magistrates' court prior to the imposition of a binding over order. By a decision of 21 October 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine) The Court ruled that the application was not admissible, and that it was not part of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) The application was made under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was “bound over’ in his own recognisance of 50 pounds sterling (GBP) together with a surety of GBP 250. The precise terms of the order were found by the Divisional Court (in the later judicial review proceedings) to be unclear. The applicant was committed to custody on the same day for 28 days. He remained in custody until 16 January 1997 or a little later. On 2 June 1997 the applicant was granted leave to apply for judicial review of the decision to impose the binding over order. The application was granted on 20 January 1998. The judges of the Court of Appeal agreed the order had been procedurally irregular and granted a declaration to that effect. Mr Justice Mance quoted headnote of case of R. v. Central Criminal Court ex parte Boulding [1984] 1 QB 813. A surety required the separate approval of the court as to his suitability. The High Court accepted that the applicant's representative was effectively presented with a ‘fait accompli’ of a nature which she had not come across before. The magistrate did not expressly invite or give opportunity for any submissions, or indeed any discussion between the applicant and his representative, about the proposed terms of the binding over order before he imposed it. The application was upheld by the High Court. Mr Justice Mance said that had the applicant or his representative been able to make submissions about the proposed order the magistrate might have been persuaded to impose different terms. He said that it seems to me certainly not beyond the bounds of possibility, that if a proper opportunity had been given to [the applicant's counsel] to consider and address the matter after brief discussion. This is all, of course, speculative, but speculation though it may be, the reason why it is speculation is that the magistrate failed, in my judgment, to give the applicant proper time or a proper chance to address the terms of the proposed bind over order.”

Behr, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The first applicant himself was hit with a truncheon on the head, which resulted in a bleeding laceration of 3cm behind his ear. The applicants had requested that they be interviewed, as the evidence had suggested that the alleged perpetrators had belonged to one of these three squads. The applicants appealed and pointed out that the members of the deployed squads had still not been questioned and that the inspected videos were fragmentary, but nonetheless contradicted certain parts of the statements made by the squad leaders. The court held that the investigations had been conducted diligently, but had not established sufficient suspicion of criminal conduct on the part of specific police officers. eval_texts: 18 Swedish nationals lodged an application with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that they had been denied effective access to court in relation to decisions taken on the construction of a railway, in violation of their rights under Articles 6 and 8 of the convention. The application was communicated to the Government on 21 May 2012. The case originated in an application (no. 29878/09) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged on 4 June 2009. On 15 October 1999, the National Rail Administration (Banverket; hereinafter “the NRA”) applied to the government for permission, under the Environmental Code (Miljöbalken), to construct a 10 km long railway section. The proposed railway construction concerned certain areas which were or were going to be part of Natura 2000. The Government stated, inter alia, that the activity could be permitted, despite its harmful effect on the environment. The property owners claimed that the decision contradicted Swedish law as well as applicable European Union law, including the Habitats Directive. A number of individual property owners, including three of the applicants in the present case, petitioned the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) for a judicial review of the case and requested that the Government’s decision be quashed. The decision was made on 12 June 2003 and allowed the construction of the railway in the proposed “corridor”. In 2003 and 2004 the NRA applied to the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) in the County of Västerbotten for a permit to construct the railway in the specific Natura 2000 area. The Environmental Court decided to examine the cases jointly. By judgments of 24 May 2005 and 13 June 2005, considering itself bound by the Government’s decision of 12 June 2003 on the permissibility of the railway project, the court decided to grant all the permits requested by the NRA. On 15 June 2006 the Environmental Court of Appeal (Miljööverdomstolen) in Stockholm quashed the judgments and referred the cases back to the latter instance. On 21 June 2005 the NRA adopted a railway plan for the area in question. 12 applicants – all but Ms Holmström, Mr Härestål and Mr Höjer – appealed to the Government against the railway plan. They essentially complained of the specific stretch of the railway, invoking nuisance such as noise and vibrations affecting the enjoyment of their property. The Supreme Administrative Court, after having held a hearing in the case, rejected the petition, finding that the railroad plan was in line with the EU Habitats Directive. Proceedings on adoption of railway plan on 19 June 2005 were held at the Royal Court of Justice in Stockholm. The court considered that the question of permissibility of a railway project was within the power of the Government. The Government’s decision was binding for the subsequent proceedings in that courts and other decision-making bodies could not examine issues that had been determined by that decision. The court, in the instant case, should have examined all the objections presented by the appellants, including the claim that there were better alternative locations for the railway. According to the dissenting judge, a full judicial review had also been foreseen by the court in its earlier decision. Compensation and others measures taken by the Government have been described as ‘futile’. At least ten of the applicants have received some form of compensation as a consequence of the railway construction. In one case, the change to noise-reducing windows was partly paid by the NRA. In the vicinity of some properties, whose owners have not received compensation, noise barriers have been erected in order to keep the noise from the railway below the applicable target values. It is not clear whether the other applicants requested compensation.
